subject: chemistry
title: Life cycle assessment and recycling
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Life cycle assessment and recycling — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.10.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Life cycle assessment and recycling, specification section 4.10.2.
final_note: You worked through Life cycle assessment and recycling — 13 specification statements.

concepts.term: Life cycle assessment (LCA)
concepts.def: An assessment carried out to judge the environmental impact of a product in each of four stages: extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation during its lifetime; and disposal at the end of its useful life, including transport and distribution at each stage.

concepts.term: Stage 1: extracting and processing raw materials
concepts.def: The first stage assessed in an LCA. It covers obtaining the raw material from the Earth or from living things and every process needed to turn it into a usable material, for example mining an ore and reducing it to the metal, or drilling for crude oil and processing it into a polymer.

concepts.term: Stage 2: manufacturing and packaging
concepts.def: The second stage assessed in an LCA. It covers making the product itself from the processed material and also producing the packaging the product is sold or transported in.

concepts.term: Stage 3: use and operation during its lifetime
concepts.def: The third stage assessed in an LCA. It covers the impact of the product while it is in use, for example the electricity and water a washing machine uses, or the detergents needed to wash a bottle that is refilled.

concepts.term: Stage 4: disposal at the end of its useful life
concepts.def: The fourth stage assessed in an LCA. It covers what happens once the product is no longer wanted, for example collection, landfill, incineration, or collection and processing for recycling.

concepts.term: Transport and distribution in an LCA
concepts.def: Moving materials, parts and finished products around is not a separate stage of an LCA. It is included at each stage, so the impact of transport and distribution is counted from raw material to final disposal.

concepts.term: Quantities that are fairly easily quantified
concepts.def: Use of water, use of resources, use of energy sources and production of some wastes can be fairly easily quantified in an LCA, because they can be measured or calculated as amounts.

concepts.term: Value judgement in an LCA
concepts.def: A decision about how much importance to give to something, made by the person carrying out the assessment rather than by measurement. Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects is less straightforward than measuring water or energy use and requires value judgements.

concepts.term: LCA is not a purely objective process
concepts.def: Because value judgements are needed to put numbers on pollutant effects, two people assessing the same product can reach different conclusions. An LCA is therefore not purely objective, even though parts of it rest on measured data.

concepts.term: Selective or abbreviated LCA
concepts.def: A shortened assessment that looks at only some stages of a product's life, or only some of the impacts. Selective or abbreviated LCAs can be devised to evaluate a product, but leaving parts out changes the conclusion that is reached.

concepts.term: Misuse of LCAs to reach pre-determined conclusions
concepts.def: A selective or abbreviated LCA can be misused by choosing in advance the conclusion that is wanted and then including only the stages or impacts that support it, for example in support of claims made for advertising purposes.

concepts.term: Comparative LCA of plastic and paper shopping bags
concepts.def: A simple side-by-side assessment of two products across the same four stages. For plastic and paper bags this means comparing raw materials (crude oil against wood), the energy and water used in manufacture, how many times each bag is used, and what happens to each bag at disposal.

concepts.term: Reduction in use, reuse and recycling by end users
concepts.def: Three distinct actions taken by the people who use products. All three reduce the use of limited resources, the use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts. Reduction in use means needing fewer products; reuse means using the same product again; recycling means processing a material into something new.

concepts.term: Limited raw materials
concepts.def: Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are produced from limited raw materials, and much of the energy for the processes also comes from limited resources.

concepts.term: Environmental impacts of quarrying and mining
concepts.def: Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying and mining causes environmental impacts, such as damage to the landscape and habitats, noise and dust, and the waste rock and other wastes produced.

concepts.term: Reuse
concepts.def: Using a product again in the form it already has. Some products, such as glass bottles, can be reused, for example by washing and refilling them.

concepts.term: Recycling for a different use
concepts.def: Processing a material so that it can be made into something new. Glass bottles can be crushed and melted to make different glass products, and products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use.

concepts.term: Recycling metals
concepts.def: Metals can be recycled by melting them and then recasting or reforming them into different products.

concepts.term: Separation required for recycling
concepts.def: The amount of separation required before a material is recycled depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product. A product that must have a precise composition needs more careful separation than one that does not.

concepts.term: Scrap steel added to iron from a blast furnace
concepts.def: Some scrap steel can be added to iron from a blast furnace. This reduces the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore, so less ore is mined and less ore has to be reduced.

concepts.term: Evaluating ways of reducing the use of limited resources
concepts.def: Weighing up the benefits and drawbacks of an option using the information given, rather than assuming one option is always best. An evaluation considers the resources, energy and water used, the waste produced and the environmental impacts, and reaches a supported conclusion.

mcqs.q: A life cycle assessment of a product assesses its environmental impact in which stages?
options: Manufacturing and packaging only, because that is the stage that uses the most energy
Extraction, manufacture, use and disposal, with transport assessed as a separate stage
Extracting the raw materials and disposal, because these are the two polluting stages
Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, disposal
mcqs.explain: These are the four stages named in the specification, with transport and distribution included at each of them.

mcqs.q: Why does a manufacturer carry out a life cycle assessment on a new product?
options: To work out the profit that will be made from selling the product
To measure the pollution released by the factory where it is made
To produce one objective score that ranks the product against all others
To assess the environmental impact of the product at every stage of its life
mcqs.explain: This is the purpose given in the specification: to assess environmental impact in each of the four stages.

mcqs.q: A poly(ethene) carrier bag is made from crude oil. Which of these belongs to the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage of its LCA?
options: Wrapping the finished bags into bundles to be sent out to the shops
Only the drilling of the crude oil, because processing is a later stage
Drilling for crude oil and cracking a fraction of it to obtain ethene
Collecting used bags from households so that they can be sorted out
mcqs.explain: Both obtaining the raw material and processing it into a usable material fall in stage 1.

mcqs.q: Finished paper bags are put into cardboard boxes at the factory before being sent to shops. In an LCA of the paper bags, this belongs to:
options: no stage at all, because packaging is thrown away and is not the product
manufacturing and packaging, with the transport counted at that same stage
a separate transport stage, which is added on after the disposal stage
use and operation, because the boxes are used by the shop receiving them
mcqs.explain: Producing packaging sits in stage 2, and transport and distribution are included at each stage.

mcqs.q: A glass milk bottle is washed and refilled every week. Which of these belongs to the 'use and operation during its lifetime' stage of its LCA?
options: The energy used to melt the sand and shape the bottle at the works
Nothing, because a bottle is not powered and so has no use stage
The water and the energy used to wash the bottle before refilling
The energy used to melt the glass down when the bottle is finished
mcqs.explain: What a product consumes each time it is used is exactly the use and operation stage.

mcqs.q: An empty steel food can is put out for kerbside recycling collection. In an LCA of the can, the impact of this is:
options: zero, because a can that is sent off for recycling is never disposed of
counted only within a separate stage covering all transport of the can
part of the disposal stage, including transporting the collected cans
part of the manufacturing stage, because the metal will be melted again
mcqs.explain: Recycling is a route at the end of the can's useful life, and transport is counted at that stage.

mcqs.q: How are transport and distribution treated in a life cycle assessment?
options: They are included at each stage of the life cycle
They form a fifth stage, placed after final disposal
They are counted only when raw materials are moved
They are left out, because they are hard to measure
mcqs.explain: The specification says 'including transport and distribution at each stage'.

mcqs.q: Which of these can be quantified fairly easily in a life cycle assessment?
options: The value that society places on protecting a nearby woodland
The harm done to a river by a pollutant released from the works
The overall objective score showing which of two products is best
The volume of water used and the waste produced in manufacture
mcqs.explain: Use of water, resources, energy sources and production of some wastes can be fairly easily quantified.

mcqs.q: Why is a life cycle assessment not a purely objective process?
options: Different scientists choose different stages of a product's life
Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires judgements
Water use, energy use and waste produced cannot be measured at all
Two assessments of one product can never produce the same figures
mcqs.explain: This is the reason given in the specification for LCA not being purely objective.

mcqs.q: A drinks company publishes an LCA of its bottle that covers the manufacturing stage only. Why is this a problem?
options: An abbreviated LCA uses the same data, so it gives the same result
An LCA is scientific, so a conclusion drawn from it must be correct
A selective LCA can be used to reach a conclusion decided in advance
Manufacturing has no environmental impact that is worth reporting
mcqs.explain: The specification warns that selective or abbreviated LCAs can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions.

mcqs.q: An advert states that a paper cup is 'proven by science to be the greenest choice'. What is the best response to this claim?
options: The claim must be true, because an LCA is a scientific process
The LCA behind the claim may be selective and should be checked
Paper products are always better, so the claim needs no checking
No LCA can ever support a claim made for advertising purposes
mcqs.explain: LCAs can be misused in support of claims for advertising purposes, so the basis of the claim must be examined.

mcqs.q: In a simple comparative LCA of plastic and paper shopping bags, which comparison is the fairest?
options: The impact per use, taking account of how often each bag is used
The cost of each bag to the shop, since price reflects resource use
The impact of making one bag, since reuse is not a part of an LCA
Whether the bag is paper, since paper is the greener material used
mcqs.explain: The two bags last different lengths of time, so impact per use is the fair basis for comparison.

mcqs.q: Making a paper bag needs 4 times as much energy as making a plastic bag. On average a plastic bag is used 20 times and a paper bag 3 times. Which conclusion follows from these figures?
options: The paper bag is better, because paper is the more natural material
Per use, the paper bag needs more energy than the plastic bag does
The two bags are equal, since the number of uses is not counted
Per use, the plastic bag needs four times the energy of the paper
mcqs.explain: Taking one unit of energy per plastic bag: plastic is 1/20 per use, paper is 4/3 per use, so paper is higher.

mcqs.q: Reduction in use, reuse and recycling of materials by end users reduces:
options: waste only, because recycling a material uses no energy of its own
the price of the products, but not the quantity of raw material used
waste and energy use, but only for reuse rather than for recycling
use of limited resources, use of energy sources, waste and impacts
mcqs.explain: These are the four things the specification says all three actions reduce.

mcqs.q: A family have the same glass bottle washed and refilled with milk each week. This is an example of:
options: recycling, because the bottle is kept out of landfill waste
reduction in use, because fewer bottles are melted down
disposal, because the bottle will be thrown away one day
reuse, because the bottle itself is used again as a bottle
mcqs.explain: The object stays intact and is used again for the same purpose, which is reuse.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the materials used to make everyday products is correct?
options: Only plastics are limited, because metal ores can always be mined
All of the energy for making these materials comes from unlimited sources
Metals, glass, ceramics and most plastics come from limited materials
Clay ceramics are limited, but glass and metals can be remade freely
mcqs.explain: The specification lists metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics together.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an environmental impact of obtaining raw materials by quarrying and mining?
options: Habitats are destroyed and waste rock and dust are produced on site
The only effect is that the landscape is left looking less attractive
There is no lasting impact, since the Earth's supply is unlimited
The ore that is left behind holds a lower percentage of metal
mcqs.explain: Quarrying and mining damage land and habitats and generate large amounts of waste rock and dust.

mcqs.q: Used glass bottles are collected, crushed and melted to make glass jars. This is best described as:
options: recycling, because the glass is processed into a new product
reuse, because the same glass is being used a second time
reduction in use, because fewer new jars need to be bought
impossible, because glass can only be remade into bottles
mcqs.explain: The bottle is destroyed and the glass is made into a different glass product, which is recycling.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between reusing a glass bottle and recycling it?
options: There is no difference; crushing and melting glass counts as reuse
Recycling means the melted glass has to be made into bottles again
Reusing keeps the bottle whole; recycling melts it into new glass
Reusing means the bottle goes to landfill after one further use
mcqs.explain: Reuse uses the object again as it is; recycling processes the material into a different product.

mcqs.q: How are metals recycled?
options: They are heated with carbon to reduce them back into the metal
They are melted and then recast or reformed into new products
They must first be separated into completely pure single metals
They are cleaned and reshaped without any energy being required
mcqs.explain: This is the method given in the specification for recycling metals.

mcqs.q: How much separation of scrap metal is needed before it is recycled?
options: It depends on the material and the properties the product needs
Complete separation is always required before any metal is melted
None is ever needed, because melting removes all the other metals
It depends only on how much scrap a blast furnace is able to take
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the amount of separation required depends on both of these.

mcqs.q: Why is some scrap steel added to iron from a blast furnace?
options: It cuts the amount of iron that must be extracted from iron ore
It removes the need for any iron ore to be used in the process
It lets the scrap be used without separating any of it beforehand
It makes the iron ore easier to reduce inside the blast furnace
mcqs.explain: This is exactly the reason given in the specification for adding scrap steel.

mcqs.q: A town council wants to reduce the use of limited resources. Which action would achieve this?
options: Sending household waste to landfill rather than to an incinerator
Setting up a scheme to collect and refill glass milk bottles
Switching to newly made plastic bottles, as plastic is unlimited
Adding more iron ore to the blast furnace in place of scrap steel
mcqs.explain: Reuse by end users reduces the use of limited resources, energy sources, waste and impacts.

mcqs.q: A council compares two ways of supplying drinks: refillable glass bottles that are collected and washed, or cans made from recycled aluminium. Which point belongs in a fair evaluation?
options: Recycling the cans uses no energy, so this option has no impact
Refilling a bottle counts as recycling, so the options are equal
Only the cost to the council matters when resources are limited
Washing the bottles uses water and energy, which must be weighed
mcqs.explain: The use stage of a reusable bottle has real impacts, and an evaluation must weigh them against the benefits.
